meta.title: Who really said "Don't be in a hurry to condemn because he doesn't do what you do or think as you think or as fast. There was a time when you didn't know what you know today"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not from a speech. The only record of this Malcolm X line is Maya Angelou's 1986 memoir, where she recalls him saying it — in slightly longer words.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't be in a hurry to condemn because he doesn't do what you do or think as you think or as fast. There was a time when you didn't know what you know today'?
meta.ogDescription: Malcolm X very likely said it — to Maya Angelou, in a car in Accra in 1964. But the wording online is trimmed, and no speech or book of his carries it.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1925–1965 · Muslim minister, Black nationalist and human-rights activist
answer.sourceLine: No speech transcript, essay or book of Malcolm X’s is known to carry this line. Its one documented appearance is in Maya Angelou’s memoir All God’s Children Need Traveling Shoes (Random House, 1986) ↗, where she recalls him saying it to her in Accra — and her printed wording is slightly longer than the version that circulates.

source.heading: The one place it is written down

docMeta.dd: All God’s Children Need Traveling Shoes
Maya Angelou · Random House, New York, 1986
Accra, Ghana, 1964 — Angelou driving Malcolm X to the airport
A memoirist’s recollection, not a transcript

source.excerpt: Malcolm said, “Sister, listen and listen carefully. Picture American racism as a mountain…” — and, further on: “… strata of American life and we are being attacked on each one. We need people on each level to fight our battle. Don’t be in such a hurry to condemn a person because he doesn’t do what you do, or think as you think or as fast. There was a time when you didn’t know what you know today.” His voice had become more explanatory and less accusatory.
trail: Wikiquote does not place this among Malcolm X’s sourced speeches and books. It sits in the Attributed section ↗, annotated “Quoted by Maya Angelou” and pointing to two second-hand printings: Conyers and Smallwood’s Malcolm X: An Historical Reader (Carolina Academic Press, 2008), p. 181, and Elaine Slivinski Lisandrelli’s Maya Angelou: More than a poet (Enslow, 1996), p. 90.

Full-text search of scanned books runs the trail back to Angelou herself: Open Library’s search-inside ↗ returns the sentence from every scanned edition of All God’s Children Need Traveling Shoes, and from the later biographies and readers that quote her.

Wikipedia’s featured article on the memoir places the scene: Malcolm X visited Ghana in 1964, and while Angelou drove him to the airport ↗ he “chastises her for her bitterness about Du Bois’ wife Shirley Graham’s lack of support for the civil rights movement.”
The estate’s own site is no help at all: malcolmx.com ↗ prints the trimmed internet wording with no citation — the same sourceless form the aggregators carry.
source.cutTag: Ellipses mark text the snippet view does not expose
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the scanned 1986 Random House edition through Open Library’s full-text search ↗, which returns the passage in short windows; the gaps are text the search view withholds, not editorial cuts. One exception, marked here rather than folded in: the closing sentence — “His voice had become more explanatory and less accusatory” — is not returned by the search inside the Random House scan. It is reproduced from the one scan whose window does expose it, Pamela Loos’s Maya Angelou (Chelsea House), quoting the same passage.

source.rightsNote: Malcolm X spoke the words, but the only fixed text of them belongs to Maya Angelou: All God’s Children Need Traveling Shoes was first published by Random House in 1986, so the passage is firmly in copyright in the United States. Treat it as her reported speech, quote it short, and credit both.

author.name: Malcolm X
author.heading: Who was Malcolm X?
author.metaLine: 1925–1965 · Muslim minister and Black nationalist leader
author.bio: Born Malcolm Little in 1925, he became the most electrifying minister of the Nation of Islam and, after leaving it, an independent voice for Black self-determination — “an African American revolutionary, civil rights activist, and Muslim minister,” as Wikipedia sums him up. In 1964 he travelled through Egypt, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Ghana, Guinea and half a dozen other African countries, meeting officials and courting the newly independent governments; the Ghana leg is where Maya Angelou says these words were spoken. He was assassinated on 21 February 1965, at thirty-nine.

cite.sourceCitation: Maya Angelou, All God’s Children Need Traveling Shoes (New York: Random House, 1986), recalling Malcolm X’s words to her in Accra, Ghana, 1964. Filed under “Attributed” in Wikiquote’s Malcolm X entry; no speech or text by Malcolm X himself is known to carry the line.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost in the copying
misattribution.intro: The name on this one is probably right. What is wrong is almost everything around it — the wording, the missing source, and the impression that it comes from a speech.

items.why: Angelou printed “Don’t be in such a hurry to condemn a person because he doesn’t do what you do, or think as you think or as fast.” The version on Goodreads ↗ and the aggregators drops “such” and “a person”.
Even the estate-managed malcolmx.com ↗ lists it as a bare quotation, with no speech, date, book or page attached.
Wikiquote ↗ keeps it out of its sourced sections for Malcolm X Speaks, the Autobiography and the 1962–65 speeches, filing it under Attributed with the note “Quoted by Maya Angelou.”

misattribution.truthLine: The honest version: Malcolm X said something very close to this, in a car in Accra in 1964, and the only person who wrote it down was Maya Angelou — in a memoir published in 1986 ↗.

context.heading: Why he said it
lead: Angelou was living in Accra when Malcolm X came through Ghana in 1964, looking for allies among Africa’s newly independent governments. She had been bitter about Shirley Graham — W. E. B. Du Bois’s wife — and her lack of support for the American civil rights movement, and she said so while driving him to the airport. The rebuke came back at her from the passenger seat.

The answer she remembered is not a greeting-card plea for tolerance. It is organising advice, and the famous sentence is only its tail: picture racism as a mountain attacked at every level, so you need people working at every level, so do not write off the ones cutting a different seam. The internet kept the kind part and quietly dropped the strategy.
context.detailsSummary: What the fuller passage actually says
detailsBody: Angelou’s narration around the line is as telling as the line. Just before it she is, in her words, “the object of his displeasure”; a passenger named Julian shifts in an uncomfortable seat; a voice in the car says “Keep your eyes on the road.” Then: “Sister, listen and listen carefully.”

Just after it, in the passage as reproduced by her biographer Pamela Loos: “His voice had become more explanatory and less accusatory.” The correction lands, then softens. That shape is probably why the sentence travels so well by itself — and why it reads flatter without the mountain that comes before it.
context.pull: “We need people on each level to fight our battle.”
